Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Negative Appraisals: Hopelessness: I have no future, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Vignette:
Adebayo, a psychologist of thirty-seven, had built his life around the quiet, contained space of the therapy room. He had always found a gentle power in its predictable safety, but for the last eight months, that same space had become a source of profound dread. The story of how this happened began at a professional conference in a city he didn't know. He’d had dinner with a senior colleague, a man he respected, and had accepted an invitation for a nightcap in the hotel bar. The details after that were fragmented, slippery images that ambushed him without warning: the unfamiliar floral pattern of a hotel room carpet coming into sharp focus, the weight of a body, the metallic click of a deadbolt sliding into place. He remembered the man’s voice, a low murmur of cruel commentary that twisted a moment of utter violation into something even more psychologically searing.

In the weeks that followed, Adebayo’s own mind, the very tool of his trade, became a hostile environment. The world was suddenly filled with threats he had never noticed before. He found he could no longer sit in a restaurant or a coffee shop unless he could secure a seat in a corner, his back pressed firmly against the wall, where no one could approach him from behind. At his practice, this vigilance became an exhausting, full-time job. He would arrange his own chair so that he had a clear view of the door and the entire room, a subtle shift he was sure his clients noticed. He had come to believe that he was transparent, that the shame of what had happened was written on his face for anyone to see. He would catch a client’s look of empathy and mistake it for a sign that they could see his weakness, his contamination. This feeling of being exposed was a constant, humiliating hum beneath the surface of every interaction.

Sleep offered no respite. The moment he tried to let go, his body would flood with adrenaline, convinced that to sleep was to be vulnerable. He would lie awake for hours, straining to hear any sound from outside his apartment, his mind replaying the click of that hotel room lock. He was perpetually exhausted, but the idea of relaxing felt impossible, a luxury he could no longer afford. He was certain that he was fundamentally helpless, that the world was a dangerous place and he possessed no ability to protect himself from the bad things that could happen at any moment.

His work, once a source of meaning, became a landscape of triggers. The click of his office door closing at the start of a session sent a jolt of panic through him. He started leaving it slightly ajar, a breach of confidentiality that gnawed at his professional conscience. Being alone with his male clients became an exercise in sheer terror. During one session, a man speaking about his own father’s anger shifted in his seat, and Adebayo flinched so visibly that the client stopped, asking if he was alright. Adebayo felt the facade of the competent therapist crumble, replaced by the certainty that this man, and every other, could see straight through him. He began referring his male clients to colleagues, citing a lack of specific expertise. The list of excuses grew, and with it, a hollowing sense of professional failure. The final straw came during a staff meeting where a colleague made an off-hand, crude joke about a recent sexual assault case in the news. Trapped in the small, windowless conference room, Adebayo felt the air thicken, the walls close in. He fled the room, gasping for breath in the hallway, the quiet concern of his colleagues feeling like a hot brand of shame on his skin.

Adebayo sought therapy feeling that his future had been erased. The career he had painstakingly built felt like a ruin, and the prospect of intimacy felt like a cruel joke. He saw his life as a series of closed doors, locked rooms he could no longer enter. What frightened him most was the thought that this was permanent, that he would never again feel safe in the world or in his own body. His hope was a small, fragile thing: to one day be able to sit in a quiet room with another person, hear the door click shut, and feel nothing at all.
